hints: Remember ser-lys means serine provides the carboxyl group and lysine provides the amino group, with water lost between $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NH}_2$.
Focus on displaying the new $\text{CONH}$ linkage clearly while keeping both side chains, $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2$, unchanged.
walkthrough:
Decide which ends join**
Think of the name ser-lys like reading left to right. The left amino acid, serine, uses its $\text{COOH}$ end, and the right amino acid, lysine, uses its $\text{NH}_2$ end. Joining $\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{N}$ loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and makes the amide peptide link.

Build the full skeleton**
Write serine as $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CO}-$ and lysine as $-\text{NHCH}((\text{CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$. Put them together to give $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CONHCH}((\text{CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$. Show the $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ of the $\text{CONH}$ group displayed, and leave the side chain $\text{-NH}_2$ of lysine free.

Final answer: Ser-lys dipeptide: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})\text{CONHCH}((\text{CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$
Peptide bond $\text{C(=O)NH}$ must be displayed with adjacent $\text{CH}$ groups correct on both sides.

hints: Think about what happens to the positive and negative charges on an amino acid as pH changes, and when they exactly cancel.
walkthrough:
Picture charge versus pH**
At low pH the amino acid is protonated and positive, at high pH it is deprotonated and negative. There is one special pH in the middle where the positive and negative balance exactly, so the molecule exists mainly as a neutral zwitterion. That pH is the isoelectric point.
Final answer: The pH at which the amino acid has no overall / no net charge.

hints: Compare the buffer pH of 5.7 with the isoelectric points 5.7 for serine and 9.7 for lysine to decide which species is neutral and which is charged.
Recall that positively charged species move toward the negative electrode and neutral zwitterions stay at the origin.
For the two positively charged species, consider which has the smaller $M_r$ and so moves faster through the gel.
walkthrough:
Work out the charge of each species at pH 5.7**
Buffer pH 5.7 equals the isoelectric point of serine, so serine has zero net charge. Lysine has isoelectric point 9.7, so at the much more acidic pH 5.7 its basic side chain and amino group are protonated, giving an overall positive charge. The dipeptide ser-lys still contains the basic lysine side chain, so it is also positively charged at pH 5.7.

Predict direction of movement**
In electrophoresis only charged species migrate. Neutral serine stays where it was applied, at x. Positively charged lysine and ser-lys are attracted toward the negative electrode on the right, so both spots shift to the right of x.

Separate lysine from ser-lys by size**
Both migrants have similar positive charge, but lysine, $M_r$ about 146, is much smaller than the dipeptide ser-lys, $M_r$ about 233. The smaller ion moves faster with less friction, so lysine travels furthest toward the negative pole, with ser-lys in the middle.

Final answer: Serine stays at origin (x), ser-lys moves part way toward negative (-) electrode, lysine moves furthest toward negative (-) electrode.
Serine is at its isoelectric point so neutral / zwitterionic with no movement; ser-lys and lysine are below their isoelectric points so positively charged and move to negative pole.
Lysine moves furthest as it has lower $M_r$ / smaller size than ser-lys.

hints: Recognise P as a cyclic amide (lactam) and Q as its hydrolysis product, so break the $\text{CO-NH}$ bond and add the elements of water.
walkthrough:
Open the lactam to find Q**
P is a six membered cyclic amide containing an $\text{-OH}$ group. Hydrolysis in step 1 breaks the $\text{CO-NH}$ bond by adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ across it. The carbonyl carbon becomes a carboxylic acid $\text{COOH}$ and the nitrogen becomes a primary amine $\text{NH}_2$. Keeping the carbon skeleton gives $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(COOH)-CH}_2\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_2\text{-NH}_2$, which matches $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{NO}_3$. This is a hydroxy amino acid that can later cyclise to the lactone R.
Final answer: Q: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{COOH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{NO}_3$, with $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ displayed.

hints: For step 1, think of the standard reagents to hydrolyse an amide to a carboxylic acid and amine.
For step 2, think of how a hydroxy acid forms an ester, especially a cyclic ester, and what dehydrating conditions drive it.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the amide in step 1**
Amides need vigorous acid hydrolysis. Use dilute aqueous acid, $\text{HCl(aq)}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}$, with heating under reflux. Water provides the $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-H}$ to split the $\text{CO-N}$ bond in P to give the amino acid Q.

Close the lactone in step 2**
Q has both $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{OH}$ in the same molecule, so heating forms an intramolecular ester (lactone) R with loss of water. This esterification is catalysed by concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with strong heating, which also acts as a dehydrating agent to drive the equilibrium toward R.

Final answer: step 1: aqueous $\text{HCl}$ or aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat / reflux
step 2: conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst, heat / high temperature
